reader.title: Reported lynching of Press Sams
bases: The only violence in the coverage is a deputy's intimation that Sams was lynched [A5][A6] and a report that he fled to escape lynching [A7]; no other act against him is reported.

The lynching rests on Deputy Sheriff McCoy's refusal to say what became of Sams while intimating he was lynched [A5][A6]; the same dispatch carries a Clinton report that he left the country, and other reports say he fled or deserted his wife before her arrest [A4][A7][A11][A16].
McCoy's intimation of a lynching [A5][A6] is contradicted by reports that Sams fled, was a fugitive, or had deserted Flack and left for parts unknown [A4][A7][A11][A16].

summary.text: The reported lynching of Press Sams was a rumor, carried in wire reports of October 1-2, 1888, that a Black coachman who had married Hattie Flack, a white merchant's daughter from near Jacksonville, Illinois, had been lynched by whites near Clinton, Kentucky.
The story rested on Deputy Sheriff D. C. McCoy, who brought Flack home to St. Louis and would not say what had become of Sams but intimated that he had been lynched.
Other reports, including a dispatch from Clinton, said Sams had fled or had deserted his wife before her arrest, and no confirmation of a killing appears in the coverage.

In mid-September 1888 Hattie B. Flack, daughter of the St. Louis commission merchant Charles E. Flack, eloped with Sams, whom a Jacksonville dispatch named "Preston Sands, a colored man" employed by the family for years.
That dispatch said he had recently been discharged for stealing, and that the couple took out a license at Springfield and drove over the line at night to marry.
The Cleveland Gazette described the bride as a pretty, eighteen-year-old seminary graduate and the groom as "one John Sams, a coal black Negro and her father's hired man."
McCoy, a deputy sheriff of Jacksonville and a friend of the family, went to Kentucky on Sams' trail and found the couple living with the family of Sams' brother-in-law.
A dispatch from Clinton said Flack was arrested on Saturday night, September 29, at Moscow, in the house of Jim Gholson, and refused to go until she learned the officers held a warrant for her.
According to the Philadelphia Press special, she gave way only after McCoy convinced her that Sams had another wife he had never divorced.
Back in St. Louis on October 1, McCoy turned Flack over to her father.

He "refuses to say what became of Sams," the special reported, "but intimates that he was lynched to save the state the expense of his trial for bigamy"; a California version of the dispatch said the lynchers were "the whites of the district."
No report of a body, an inquest or any arrest was found.
Flack, an Indianapolis paper said, "now bitterly repents her folly."
The story reached readers mainly as a tale about the bride, under headlines such as "Miss Flack's Infatuation," "She Likes Color," "Tired of Her Negro Husband" and "Wasn't Even an Honest Negro."

Only the Philadelphia Press special, reprinted by the Washington Evening Star and the Wheeling Intelligencer, put the lynching in its headline: "She Married the Negro Coachman, and He Has Probably Been Lynched."
The shorter St. Louis item that ran in Indianapolis, Memphis, Omaha and Alexandria on October 2 turned the rumor around, saying Sams "fled to escape lynching."
The Clinton dispatch, printed in Annapolis, Richmond and Wheeling, made no mention of a lynching and said only that Sams had deserted his wife.
The St. Paul Western Appeal ran the same dispatch on October 6 in a column of news "Pertaining to Colored People," calling Sams "a Colored man" where other papers printed "a negro."
None of the papers commented on the reported lynching itself; the reports dwelt on Flack, her family and Sams' character.
Accounts of Sams' fate disagree: McCoy implied a lynching, yet the same special noted that "the report given out at Clinton is that Sams has left the country."

A Rock Island paper called him "a horse thief" and "now a fugitive in Kentucky," while the Superior Times said he had left her the week before "for parts unknown," after pawning her clothing, and had served four years for horse stealing and had a wife at Union City, Tennessee.
The Clinton dispatch is the only report datelined near the scene, and it places his departure before the arrest; the lynching account rests on what McCoy hinted but would not state.

framing.detail: The Philadelphia Press special, headed 'She Married the Negro Coachman, and He Has Probably Been Lynched', passed on McCoy's intimation without comment.
Headlines mocked the marriage and Sams ('Wasn't Even an Honest Negro', 'She Likes Color', 'Tired of Her Negro Husband'), and the St. Louis item said 'the girl now bitterly repents her folly.'
The St. Paul Western Appeal ran the Clinton dispatch in a column of news 'Pertaining to Colored People', changing 'a negro' to 'a Colored man'.

versions.value: Had deserted Flack before her arrest; left for parts unknown the week before

conflicts.note: The Clinton-datelined dispatch is the report nearest the scene and puts Sams' departure before the arrest; the lynching rests only on what McCoy implied and would not state.

info: Flack was arrested at Moscow, Ky., on Saturday night before the Clinton dispatch of October 1, 1888 (September 29); the elopement and marriage took place about two weeks earlier.
A log cabin in the mountains near Clinton, Ky. (St. Louis dispatch), or the house of Sams' brother-in-law at Moscow, Ky. (Clinton dispatch).
Press Sams (also 'Pres Sams', 'Preston Sands', 'John Sams'; OCR 'Sama'), called a negro, mulatto or colored man, the Flack family's coachman or hired man.

Bigamy: Sams was said to have another, undivorced wife (at Union City, Tenn., per one report); McCoy intimated he was lynched to save the state the expense of a bigamy trial. He was also called a horse thief and said to have been discharged for stealing.
Per McCoy's intimation only, 'the whites of the district'; no one is named.
Unconfirmed; McCoy said Sams was 'probably' lynched, while other reports have him a fugitive or gone for parts unknown.
Hattie Flack was returned to her father in St. Louis; what became of Sams is not settled in the coverage.
